claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The standard near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a single-phase configuration.
A combinatorial Design of Experiments can be used to systematically vary the percentage of each constituent element.
The Taguchi method is an appropriate example of such a compositional Design of Experiments for HfNbTaTiZr.
Systematically varying individual elemental percentages will produce measurable differences in hardness and yield strength.
Specific elements such as Hf or Ta have a more pronounced effect on mechanical properties than the other constituents.
Compositional variations can be selected that preserve a single-phase HfNbTaTiZr microstructure.
Changing individual constituent concentrations alters lattice distortion.
Changing individual constituent concentrations alters solid-solution strengthening.
Changes in lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening influence dislocation movement and defect interactions.
Changes in dislocation movement and defect interactions affect hardness and yield strength.
Hf is an element with a comparatively large atomic size in this alloy.
Increasing the Hf percentage will produce a statistically significant increase in hardness relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Increasing the Hf percentage will produce a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Other elemental-percentage variations may produce more moderate mechanical-property changes.
The equiatomic or near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr baseline has established and reproducible mechanical properties.
There are compositional thresholds beyond which secondary phases form in HfNbTaTiZr.
Holding processing and testing conditions constant can help isolate compositional effects.
X-ray diffraction can be used to check whether the compositionally varied samples remain single phase.
A reproducible absence of statistically significant correlations between composition and mechanical properties would falsify the hypothesis.
